title: Testing rapid game prototyping with AI,,,looking for technical feedback
author: Equivalent-Spend-415
selftext:
Hey all,

I’ve been experimenting with fast iteration workflows using OneTap Build, mainly to see how viable prompt-driven design is for early gameplay testing.

Instead of building inside a traditional engine first, I used it to generate and tweak a small playable loop through structured prompts. The goal wasn’t polish - just validating:



\- pacing

\- interaction clarity

\- mechanic repetition

\- whether the core loop holds up 

\- past 2–3 minutes



Here’s the current playable test

build:

[https://engine.onetap.build/play/game-20260204-59d685e3/](https://engine.onetap.build/play/game-20260204-59d685e3/)



I’d genuinely appreciate technical thoughts:



\- Does the loop degrade too fast?

\- Is behavior logic predictable?

\- Does it feel prototype-level or closer to playable?



Not trying to hype AI here ,,, more interested in where it actually breaks down.

comments.author: Stringedbeanz
comments.body: From a workflow perspective, this is interesting. I’ve been wondering whether prompt iteration is fast enough to replace early greyboxing. This feels like it might.

replies.author: Equivalent-Spend-415
replies.body: That was basically the experiment. I didn’t treat it as a final product at all,, more like skipping the empty-scene phase and jumping straight to interaction testing.

comments.author: Kenjiroxox
comments.body: The pacing is okay but enemy behavior feels deterministic. Did you manually adjust logic or rely fully on prompts?

replies.author: Equivalent-Spend-415
replies.body: Mostly prompt adjustments. That’s actually where I hit limits precision tuning still feels easier in a traditional engine.

comments.author: sense-net-mccoy
comments.body: You are clearly trying to hype your platform.

comments.author: Historical-Doubt9091
comments.body: Loop clarity is decent for a quick build. It doesn’t feel random, which is better than most AI prototypes I’ve tried.

comments.author: iabhishekpathak7
comments.body: Not gonna lie, I expected it to feel chaotic. It’s more stable than I thought.

comments.author: Pretend-Raspberry-87
comments.body: I’ve tested similar flows in OneTap Build and iteration speed is definitely the biggest strength. Fine control still needs work though.

comments.author: Hot_Initiative3950
comments.body: Biggest question for me is scalability. Do you see this staying useful beyond prototype stage?

replies.author: Equivalent-Spend-415
replies.body: Honestly, I see it as a front-end ideation layer more than a production system. Once something works, I’d likely rebuild it traditionally.

comments.author: Afzaalch00
comments.body: I’ve used OneTap.build for similar rapid prototyping tests. The loop feels good early on, but the logic becomes readable pretty fast which makes it degrade a bit after a couple minutes. Still works well as a concept validation tool though.

comments.author: Which-Drop-6797
comments.body:
Think they have changed name to [Tessala.co](http://Tessala.co) I have used their platform for 3 weeks now. Solid stuff, I always wanted to make games but never knew coding. So pretty cool to be able to go from idea to game by just describing what you want.

I really like the game you made, reminds me of a very old school game I used to play called Achtung die curve. In that game the "trail" you left behind you would leave a small gap so you or the other player could travel through it, could be something to try.
